description:
🚀 We are CosmoVigil

We are an ambitious and creative team passionate about space exploration, biotechnology, human health, and innovative technologies.
summary:
CosmoVigil is an Android app for monitoring astronaut health on long space missions. Inside it runs AstroCheck AI: 12 small AI models that turn data from sensors astronauts already use (smartwatch, chest ECG, glucose monitor, pulse oximeter, retinal scanner and the ISS radiation dosimeter) into one daily health check. The checks cover heart, sleep, blood sugar, temperature, mood, exercise load, blood oxygen, reaction time, eye changes and radiation. Every model was tested on people it had never seen during training.

The app learns each astronaut’s personal normal over 14 days and raises a warning only when a value crosses a NASA limit and clearly departs from that person’s baseline. Inspired by our interview with Danna Karagussova, the first woman from Kazakhstan in space, every alert says what changed, how urgent it is and what to do. In 1,500 simulated missions, it caught 97% of health events with fewer than one false alarm per month.
This matters because in space health drifts slowly, and astronauts often can’t feel it. On missions to Mars, the crew will be too far away for doctors on Earth to help in real time, so they need a system that notices problems early and explains them clearly.
details:
CosmoVigil is an Android app that gives astronauts a daily health check from sensors they already wear or use on the ISS: a smartwatch, a chest-strap ECG, a continuous glucose monitor, a pulse oximeter, a thermal camera, a retinal OCT scanner and the onboard radiation dosimeter. Inside the app runs AstroCheck AI, a set of 12 small AI models that track eye changes linked to spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome, heart rate variability, heart rate, blood sugar 30 minutes ahead, body temperature, sleep, mood from a short journal entry and from a wristband, exercise load for bones and muscles, blood oxygen, reaction time and radiation. A unified alert engine reads all 12 results every day. During the first 14 days it learns each astronaut’s personal normal. After that, it raises a warning only when a value both crosses a NASA limit and clearly departs from that person’s own baseline. It also reads signals together, the way a flight surgeon would: for example, a high resting heart rate, low HRV and short sleep together point to overfatigue. Every alert, in English or Russian, says what changed, how urgent it is and what to do.

The main benefit is that slow health changes are caught before the astronaut feels them. In 1,500 simulated 120-day missions, the system caught 97.1% of health events with about 0.9 unnecessary warnings per month. Because every warning needs two independent reasons, the crew is not overwhelmed by false alarms. The system explains itself in plain language instead of showing raw numbers, and the models are small enough to run on an onboard laptop. That matters when Earth is minutes of signal delay away.

Our intended impact is to help crews on missions to the Moon and Mars manage their health without real-time help from Earth. CosmoVigil is a self-check tool, not a diagnosis, and final decisions stay with the flight surgeon. The same approach can help people on Earth who work long hours in isolated or extreme conditions, such as shift workers at remote sites, polar researchers, pilots and night-shift medical staff.

We built the models in Python with scikit-learn, NumPy, SciPy, pandas, wfdb and MNE. Most of them use gradient boosting, Extra Trees or a linear SVM. The eye model is a ResNet18 convolutional network served with ONNX Runtime. The models run behind a FastAPI service in a Docker container deployed on Render, with the code on GitHub. The app is written in Kotlin with the native Android SDK and built with Gradle and JDK 21. Our data came from the NASA ISS RadLab dosimeter archive, NASA standards such as NASA-STD-3001, Human Research Program evidence reports, and open physiological datasets including WESAD, MIT-BIH, PPG-DaLiA, Sleep-EDF and the Kermany retinal OCT dataset. We trained everything on a standard laptop and tested the app on an Android phone. We used Claude as a coding and research assistant, but the team trained all the models, and every reported number comes from our own runs.

The project is creative because it compares every astronaut with themselves rather than with a population average, which absorbs the shifts microgravity causes in everyone. The two-reason rule and the cross-signal patterns imitate how a flight surgeon actually reasons. The radiation model learns the expected dose for 1,227 orbital cells from real ISS data and is trained on solar storms built by scaling the real September 2017 event. It correctly raised an alarm during the real May 2024 solar storm. Most importantly, the design started from a real astronaut’s experience, not from a list of sensors.

We considered several factors throughout. We interviewed Danna Karagussova, the first woman from Kazakhstan in space. She told us that in flight it is hard to judge from your own feelings what matters, and that an alert must say what changed, how urgent it is and what to do. We validated honestly: every model was tested on people, or years of data, it had never seen. We did not ship models that failed this test, such as blood pressure, where the error was 16.5 mmHg, and anemia detection from an eyelid photo, which scored 0.81. We also report weak spots openly, such as reaction time at 0.81. Because apart from radiation the training data comes from people on Earth, we rely on personal baselines. Finally, we thought about privacy, so that astronauts see all their own data while the medical team receives the warnings, and about communication delay, alert fatigue and the limited time and attention of a busy crew.
